813.title: Singing the verses
813.hook: these poems were memorized and chanted for centuries before being written down
813.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, texts are memorized in Pali and chanted in a steady intoned style, the kind of chant the Vinaya allows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week closed with a crowd of voices, and a question: which voice is yours? Did you name one to someone? Today, how those voices reached us at all. Day eight hundred thirteen.

Before dawn, in the Buddha's dwelling, a teacher turns to a visiting monk and says, let the teaching come to you to speak. And the monk begins to recite from memory, in a steady, intoned voice, a whole chapter of verses, start to finish, while the teacher listens. It's in the Udana, and in the Vinaya too. Nobody in the story opens a book. Today, the elders' songs as they first lived: in the mouth and the ear.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, A MONK RECITES.` → `NO BOOK TO OPEN.` → `IN THE MOUTH AND THE EAR.`

segments.voice: First, who's reciting. His name is Sona too, Sona Kutikanna, a different monk from the Sona with the bleeding feet. He has traveled a long way to see the Buddha, and they spend the night in the same dwelling. At dawn, invited, he intones a chapter of verses from the Sutta Nipata. When he finishes, the Buddha praises him: good, monk, you've learned these well, kept them well in mind, and you speak them clearly, with a fine voice. The praise is for memory and delivery both. Second, where the line is. The Vinaya tells of monks who chanted the teaching in a long, drawn-out singing voice, the way songs are sung for entertainment. People complained. The Buddha forbids it and gives his reasons: the singer gets caught by the sound, the listeners do too, concentration breaks, and those who come later copy the style. Yet he allows intoning, a steady chant that carries the words. The voice is meant to serve the verse, not the other way around. Third, how long the voice carried them. The chronicle of Sri Lanka, the Mahavamsa, says that monks in earlier times passed down the texts and their commentary by mouth. Then, seeing that people were declining, they came together and wrote them down in books, so the teaching would last. Tradition holds that the elders' songs traveled that same road. Fourth, what that road asks of a voice. Sona was praised for memory and clear speech, and the rule against performing kept the attention on the words. In this telling, the page came late. The verses were sung before they were written, and wherever they're chanted now, a voice still carries them.
screen: `A DIFFERENT SONA, AT DAWN.` · `INTONE, DON'T PERFORM.` · `BY MOUTH, THEN IN BOOKS.` · `A VOICE STILL CARRIES THEM.` · then, large: `SUNG BEFORE WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite one poem from memory. Choose something short you already know, or the line you kept from yesterday's elder. Subhuti's will do: my hut is roofed and snug, so rain if you like. Sit up a little, and take one easy breath. Say the lines quietly, in an even voice, not performing them, just carrying them. Then say them again, a little slower. Notice where your memory slips, and where it holds. Let the words go and come back with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Singing the verses. The elders' songs lived first in the voice: memorized, intoned and passed mouth to ear, long before anyone wrote them down. Today's word.
Your line: sung before written. Today, learn four lines of something you love by heart, a poem, a verse, a song, so it goes where you go. Day eight hundred thirteen.

forbid all chanting.

fork.reveal: in the Vinaya he forbids the drawn-out singing voice, giving his reasons, and allows intoning, a chant that carries the words.

814.title: Your own verse
814.hook: the tradition of an awakening verse: a line spoken from what you've seen
814.howItsDone: The Udana is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya in the Pali canon; Theravada teachers draw on its stories and verses, and its opening verse is linked with the night of the awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a monk recited a chapter of verses at dawn, from memory. Your line was sung before written. Did four lines go into your memory? Today, where such a verse comes from in the first place. Day eight hundred fourteen.

Then, knowing the meaning of this, on that occasion, he spoke this inspired verse. That sentence, give or take, closes story after story in a small book of the Pali canon. Something happens: monks debate which of two kings is richer, boys beat a snake with a stick, a monk sits through pain without complaint. The Buddha sees it. And a verse comes out of him, not prepared, not polished, spoken because of what he just saw. The book is named after that kind of verse. Today's word: udana.
screen: `KNOWING THE MEANING OF THIS.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS, A VERSE COMES.` → `TODAY'S WORD: UDANA.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Udana is an inspired utterance: a verse that rises out of a moment of seeing. The Udana, the book, collects them, each with its story first and its verse after. Bhaddiya, sighing ah, what bliss under his tree, is one of its stories. Second, the first one. The book opens just after the awakening. The Buddha sits under the tree, and in the first part of the night he attends to how things arise from causes. Then he speaks: when things become clear to someone ardent and absorbed, his doubts all vanish, because he understands each thing along with its cause. It isn't a hymn. It's a report of what he's just seen. Third, the elders. Their songs are not all called udanas, but tradition says the elders spoke theirs the same way, on the day something came clear: Subhuti's hut, Rahula's double fortune, Nanda's plain confession. A verse spoken from seeing, not from wishing. That's what links the book and the songs. Fourth, what it isn't. An udana isn't a prayer, and it isn't a vow. It doesn't ask for anything or promise anything. It says: this is so. And the verses in this book are brief. Seeing clearly, here, doesn't take many words. That leaves room for anyone who sits, at any stage, to find a line rising out of something they've actually seen. Not a verse about awakening. A verse about the rain on the roof, or the moment the anger went quiet.
screen: `A VERSE THAT RISES FROM SEEING.` · `DOUBTS VANISH, CAUSES SEEN.` · `THE ELDERS SPOKE THE SAME WAY.` · `NOT A PRAYER, NOT A VOW.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line from your practice. Not from what you hope for, from what you've noticed. Close your eyes for a moment. Look back over these days of sitting. Was there a moment something shifted, even a little? A breath that went long on its own. A thought that let go. A sound that was just a sound. Let one moment come. Then let one plain sentence come out of it, the way the elders' lines came: this is so. Hold it in your mind until the bell, and write it down after. The bell holds the time.
Udana. An inspired utterance: a short verse spoken out of a moment of seeing, not prepared and not polished. Today's word.
Your line: your own verse. Today, keep the line you found somewhere you'll see it again, and leave it as plain as it came. Day eight hundred fourteen.

815.title: The songs, closed
815.hook: the sisters and brothers, their forests and their freedom
815.howItsDone: The Theragatha and Therigatha sit side by side in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali canon, and tradition hears in them the voices of the Buddha's early disciples.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was udana, a verse spoken out of a moment of seeing. Your line was your own verse. Is yours still where you put it? Today, the songs close. Day eight hundred fifteen.

A robe sewn by hand, and someone told to sleep softly in it. A lamp's wick drawn down. A mortar, a pestle, a crooked husband, all left behind. A flower-sweeper bowed to at sunrise. A white crane flying ahead of the storm. A lute, tuned neither too tight nor too slack. For five weeks we've listened to the elders sing. Today, the last song of the block is the whole songbook, heard once more.
screen: `A WICK, A MORTAR, A LUTE.` → `FIVE WEEKS OF SONGS.` → `THE WHOLE SONGBOOK, ONCE MORE.`

segments.voice: First, the sisters. We began with the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. A nun told to sleep softly. Punna, filling herself with good things like the moon. Mutta, so freed. Patacara watching the flame go out, then teaching women who had lost their children: you don't know where he came from or where he went. Kisa Gotami's good friends. Ambapali's black hair. Subha, Punnika, Isidasi, Sumedha, each with her own long story, told her own way. Second, the brothers. Then the Theragatha, the verses of the elder monks. Subhuti's hut. The monsoon, the peacocks and the cranes. Sunita, once despised. Angulimala, the moon coming out from behind the cloud. Kassapa's hills, Sariputta's patience, Ananda's dark directions. Third, the forests. Again and again these songs are set outdoors: in groves, on rocky hills, in the rain, at the root of a tree. The freedom they describe isn't only inside a mind. It's in a place, with weather. Fourth, the freedom itself. It sounds different in each mouth. For Mutta it's leaving a kitchen. For Bhaddiya it's living without fear. For Nanda it's being pulled out of his own vanity. The collections don't flatten them into one story. They keep the names, the moods, even the complaints. What the block leaves behind is not a doctrine stated once, but a crowd of people, women and men, saying what happened to them, in verse, for whoever would listen. The elders sang.
screen: `THE SISTERS SANG FIRST.` · `THE BROTHERS: HUTS, HILLS, MONSOON.` · `FORESTS, GROVES AND RAIN.` · `FREEDOM IN EACH MOUTH.` · then, large: `THE ELDERS SANG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one voice. Sit, and let the room go quiet around you. From all these songs, let one singer come forward. Don't choose; let one arrive. Picture where they sit: a grove, a hut, a cell with a lamp, a hillside. Let their one line sound in you, as close as you remember it. Then simply keep them company, the way you'd sit beside an old friend who doesn't need you to talk. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, just let them be near. The bell holds the time.
The songs. The verses of the elder nuns and the elder monks: forests, grief, freedom, each in its singer's own voice. Today's word.
Your line: the elders sang. Today, step outside for one minute, under a tree or in the open air, and remember where these songs were sung. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: How a Jataka works
816.hook: each tale has a present story, a past story, and a last line saying who each character was
816.howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold, painted and performed in Theravada communities, and in the collection each tale closes by saying who each character was.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the songs closed, and the elders sang one last time. Your line was the elders sang. Did you step outside for a minute? Today, a new block begins: the longer Jataka tales. Day eight hundred sixteen.

The talkative tortoise was Kokalika. The wise minister was the Bodhisatta. That's how one tale ends, in the Jataka, the great collection of stories about the Buddha's past lives. Two sentences, and suddenly a fable about a tortoise is also about a monk the listeners knew. Before we tell the longer tales over the coming weeks, today is about the frame they all share. Learn the frame once, and the tales that follow get easier to read.
screen: `THE TORTOISE WAS KOKALIKA.` → `A FABLE ABOUT SOMEONE THEY KNEW.` → `LEARN THE FRAME ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, a story in the present. A tale opens in the Buddha's own lifetime, with something that has just happened among the monks. In the tortoise tale, a monk named Kokalika has come to ruin through his own careless tongue, and the monks are talking about it. The Buddha says: this isn't the first time his tongue has brought him down. Second, a story in the past. Long ago, when a king reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha in an earlier life, was that king's minister. The king talked without stopping. Meanwhile, a tortoise made friends with two young geese, and they offered to fly him home with them, if he'd bite the middle of a stick and keep his mouth shut. Up they went. Villagers below shouted and laughed at the sight. The tortoise opened his mouth to answer back, let go of the stick, and fell into the king's courtyard. The minister used the broken tortoise to teach the king to talk less. Third, the verses. Somewhere in the tale, someone speaks a short verse, here the Bodhisatta to his king, the lesson pressed into a few lines. Fourth, who was who. Then the Buddha connects the two stories. The tortoise was Kokalika. The minister was the Bodhisatta. That last line is the hinge. It turns an old fable into a mirror: the same habits, the same people, coming round again. When you read a Jataka, you can start at the end. The last line tells you who to watch.
screen: `A STORY IN THE PRESENT.` · `A STORY IN THE PAST.` · `A VERSE WITH THE LESSON.` · `THE LAST LINE IS THE HINGE.` · then, large: `WHO WAS WHO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one Jataka's last line. Today, take the tortoise's. Get comfortable, and hold the line: the tortoise was Kokalika; the wise minister was the Bodhisatta. Now bring up one small moment from your own week, a conversation, a mistake, a kindness. Tell it as a tiny fable in your mind. Then give it a last line: who was the tortoise there, and who was the wise minister? You might be both. Don't judge the answer. Just see who was who. The bell holds the time.
How a Jataka works. A story in the present, a story in the past, verses with the lesson, and a last line saying who was who. Today's word.
Your line: who was who. Today, when a story repeats itself in your life, an old argument, a familiar mistake, notice it and ask, who was who last time? Day eight hundred sixteen.

817.title: Sumedha in the mud
817.hook: a hermit lies down in the mud so the past Buddha Dipankara can walk over him, and vows to awaken (Jataka, the introduction)
817.howItsDone: In Theravada communities the story of Sumedha and Dipankara is told as the start of the Buddha's long path, and in Mahayana communities bodhisattva vows are taken in ceremonies and recited in practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how a Jataka works: a story now, a story long ago, and a last line naming who each character was. Your line was who was who. Did you notice an old pattern showing up again? Today, the story the tales grow out of. Day eight hundred seventeen.

Mud. A stretch of road still soft and wet, and a Buddha walking toward it. The introduction to the Jataka opens long before Siddhartha, with a hermit named Sumedha. A city is preparing its road for the Buddha Dipankara, and Sumedha has asked for a piece of it to make smooth himself. He hasn't finished. The mud is still there when Dipankara and his monks arrive. So Sumedha does something nobody asked of him. That moment is today.
screen: `A ROAD NOT FINISHED.` → `A HERMIT NAMED SUMEDHA.` → `THE BUDDHA ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: First, who Sumedha was. In the story he's born rich, and one day he looks at the treasure his family left him and thinks: they gathered all this, and not one of them took a coin along when they died. So he gives it away and goes to the mountains to live as a hermit. The mud scene starts with empty hands. Second, the mud. As Dipankara comes near, Sumedha loosens his hair, spreads his rough hermit's garment over the wet ground, and lies down in it, face down, so the Buddha and the monks can walk across him and keep their feet clean. It's a strange, physical act. Not a speech. A body on a road. Third, the choice. Lying there, the text says, Sumedha knows he could end his own suffering in this very life if he wished. And he turns it down. What use is crossing over alone, he thinks. He'd rather become a Buddha himself, and carry others across with him. That's the vow: a longer road, chosen on purpose, for other people. Fourth, the answer. Dipankara stops beside him, looks far ahead, and declares that this hermit will one day be a Buddha named Gotama. The crowd hears it. Sumedha stands up. The Jataka's introduction sets the tales that follow on the long road from this vow. Mahayana traditions teach a bodhisattva vow too, in their own words and forms. In this story, the road begins with a man in the dirt, and a promise said silently.
screen: `FIRST HE GAVE IT ALL AWAY.` · `HE LAY DOWN IN THE MUD.` · `HE CHOSE THE LONGER ROAD.` · `DIPANKARA SAW AND SPOKE.` · then, large: `THE VOW IN THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one quiet vow. Not a grand one. Something small you could actually keep, aimed at someone besides yourself. Making a little more room for one person this week. Answering one message with patience. Choose it now, and say it once, silently, the way Sumedha did in the mud, with nobody watching. Then let it go and just breathe. You don't have to feel anything special. A vow can be quiet and still be real. The bell holds the time.
Sumedha in the mud. The hermit who lay down before the Buddha Dipankara and vowed to awaken, not alone, but for others. Today's word.
Your line: the vow in the mud. Once today, when there's a quick way for you and a slower way that helps someone else, notice the choice. Then pick on purpose. Day eight hundred seventeen.

818.title: The ten perfections
818.hook: generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, effort, patience, truth, resolve, kindness, equanimity: Sumedha finds each one and its picture
818.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching and chanting the ten perfections are named, and the Jataka tales are taught as examples of them; Mahayana traditions teach a related list of paramitas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sumedha lay in the mud and chose the longer road. Your line was the vow in the mud. Did you pick the slower way once, on purpose? Today, what he packs for that road. Day eight hundred eighteen.

A vow is a start, not a plan. In the Jataka's introduction, once the crowd has gone, Sumedha sits alone and asks himself a practical question: what does a person need to become a Buddha? He doesn't get a list handed to him. He searches, the story says, and finds the qualities one at a time, each with a picture from ordinary life to hold it. The tradition calls them perfections. Today, the list and its pictures.
screen: `A VOW, THEN A QUESTION.` → `HE SEARCHES ALONE.` → `ONE PICTURE FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Parami. The tradition uses it for a quality practiced until it's complete. The list Sumedha finds is generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, effort, patience, truth, resolve, kindness and equanimity. Ten. Second, the giving ones. Generosity is a water jar turned upside down: it pours out everything and keeps nothing back. Virtue is like a yak that guards its own tail, the story says, and would rather lose its life than lose that. Renunciation is a prisoner who has lived too long in a cell and wants only the open door. Third, the steady ones. Wisdom is a monk going on alms rounds who skips no house, high or low, and learns from everyone. Effort is a lion, strong in every posture. Patience is the earth, which takes whatever is thrown on it, clean or foul, and doesn't complain. Truth is the morning star, keeping its course in every season. Resolve is a rock mountain the wind can't move. Fourth, the warm and the even. Kindness is water, which cools the good and the bad alike. And equanimity is the earth again, unmoved by what it's handed, pleasant or not. What's striking is how plain the pictures are. Jars, yaks, stars, water, dirt. The Jataka tales that follow are read as these ten being practiced, one life at a time. Mahayana texts teach a related list of perfections, called paramitas, with some names in common. Either way, the qualities are offered as things you build, not things you're born with.
screen: `PARAMI: PRACTICED TO COMPLETION.` · `A JAR, A YAK, AN OPEN DOOR.` · `A LION, THE EARTH, A STAR.` · `WATER COOLS GOOD AND BAD ALIKE.` · then, large: `TEN PERFECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the ten. Slowly, one with each out-breath. Generosity. Virtue. Renunciation. Wisdom. Effort. Patience. Truth. Resolve. Kindness. Equanimity. If one slips away, let it go; the list will come back around. When you've named them, notice whether one stands out today, the one that would help most. Don't judge yourself on the others. Just let that one picture rest in your mind: the jar, the star, the water. The bell holds the time.
Parami. A perfection: a quality practiced until it's complete. Sumedha found ten, each with its own picture. Today's word.
Your line: ten perfections. Take the one that stood out and look for a single chance to practice it before tonight. One jar poured, one rock unmoved. Day eight hundred eighteen.

819.title: Two caravans
819.hook: one leader trusts spirits who say to throw away the water; the other keeps it (Jataka 1)
819.howItsDone: The Apannaka Jataka stands first in the Pali Jataka collection, and Buddhist teachers tell it as a lesson in thinking a situation through before acting on persuasive advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten perfections: a jar poured out, a star on its course, water that cools everyone. Your line was ten perfections. Which one did you practice? Today, the tale that opens the numbered collection. Day eight hundred nineteen.

Why haul all those heavy jars? There's plenty of water ahead, pools and lakes. The travelers who say it come down the desert road looking like people just out of a rainstorm: wet clothes, lotus flowers in their hair, mud on their cart wheels. They're friendly. Throw the water out, they say, and move faster. In the first tale of the Jataka, two caravans meet travelers like these. One leader listens. One doesn't.
screen: `WET CLOTHES, MUD ON THE WHEELS.` → `THROW THE WATER OUT.` → `ONE LISTENS, ONE DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: First, the two leaders. Both are merchants about to cross the same desert. One is the bodhisatta, the future Buddha. The other is a young man the tale calls foolish, eager to go first so he'll get the best grass and water along the way. The bodhisatta lets him. Second, the first caravan. Deep in the desert, the friendly travelers appear. They're really a demon and his followers in disguise, and their whole show is a trick. The young leader believes them. His people pour their water onto the sand. They walk on, find no pools at all, and by night they're too weak to resist. The demons devour the caravan. Third, the second caravan. The bodhisatta meets the same strangers, the same wet clothes, the same advice. He doesn't argue, and he doesn't panic. He reasons. There's no rain wind blowing. No storm cloud on the horizon. This is a desert that's known to be dry. And these people's eyes are red and they cast no shadow, the tale says. So he tells his caravan: not one drop is to be thrown away until we see new water with our own eyes. They walk on. They pass the bones of the first caravan. They cross safely. Fourth, the point. The tale doesn't praise suspicion for its own sake. It praises checking what's in front of you before trading away what keeps you alive. Advice that arrives wearing all the right costumes can still be wrong. The sensible habit, kept quietly, is what gets everyone home.
screen: `TWO MERCHANTS, ONE DESERT.` · `THE FIRST POURS IT OUT.` · `THE SECOND CHECKS THE SKY.` · `THE COSTUME CAN BE WRONG.` · then, large: `KEEP THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one sensible habit. Name one plain thing that keeps you steady. Sleep. A walk. A glass of water. Ten minutes without your phone. Now notice the voices that tell you to drop it: you're too busy, it doesn't matter today, there'll be plenty later. Don't fight them. Just look at the sky the way the bodhisatta did. Is there really rain ahead? Then decide, quietly, to keep the jar full today. Breathe, and let the decision settle. The bell holds the time.
Two caravans. One pours out its water on a stranger's word; one checks the sky and keeps it. Today's word.

Your line: keep the water. This week the verses were sung from memory, you found a line of your own, the songs closed, and the Jataka opened: who was who, a vow in the mud, ten perfections, two caravans. Today, when someone says drop the sensible thing, check the sky first. Day eight hundred nineteen.

fork.setup: you're leading a caravan across a dry desert. friendly travelers with wet clothes say there's water ahead and you should pour yours out to move faster. what do you do?
options: pour it out. they've clearly just seen rain.
keep every drop until you see new water yourself.
pour out half, to be safe both ways.
fork.reveal: the bodhisatta notices no rain wind and no storm cloud, keeps the water, and his caravan crosses safely past the bones of the one that listened.

original.note: Pali apannaka, the name of this first tale; translators render it as something sure or certain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about not trusting strangers.
what it means: one leader trades away his water on persuasive advice; the other checks the evidence first and keeps it.

what a scholar hears: the tale stands first in the Pali collection; its present-day frame is about followers who leave the Buddha's teaching and later return, and it's read as a lesson in reasoning before acting.
